title: What is life? Why every test for life has an exception

summary.text: A candle flame uses up wax, needs air, grows bigger and spreads to a new wick. Yet nobody calls a flame alive. A mule almost never has young, and a seed can wait for centuries without doing anything. Yet both are alive. So every simple test for life has an exception, and scientists still argue about the best definition. In this unit your child tests their own rule for life against hard cases, watches a beetroot cell lose its colour when it is heated, and finds that a living thing stays different from its surroundings by working at it all the time.
summary.art: A child at a kitchen table with a notebook, looking at a row of five things: a candle flame, a salt crystal, a mule in a drawing, a dry seed in a jar and a beetroot cube in a glass of water, with a big question mark above them.

intro.hook: A candle flame uses up wax. It needs air, because it goes out under a glass. It grows when you add a wick, and it spreads to a new wick. Is a flame alive? And what about a mule, who almost never has young, or a dry seed that does nothing at all?
intro.text: Every simple test for life gets fooled by something. A flame passes many tests and is not alive. A seed fails many tests and is alive. Scientists know this, and they have tried for a hundred years to write a better test. In this unit you will write your own rule, break it, and mend it. You will also see what happens inside a living cell when it is heated, and why staying warm in a cool room is hard work.
intro.art: A candle flame on one side and a dry moong seed on the other, with a child holding a pencil over a notebook page headed 'Alive means...'.

outcomes: I can explain why one sign of life, such as growing or moving, cannot tell living things from non-living things, using fire and crystals as examples.
I can name some tests for life that scientists use, and give an exception to each one.
I can explain that a living body stays different from its surroundings, and that this takes energy all the time.
I can explain why heating a living cell makes its colour leak out, using the idea of a skin around every cell.
I can explain how seeds and some animals can be alive while doing almost nothing, and how long a seed can wait.
I can explain why scientists disagree about whether a virus is alive.
I can write a rule for what is alive, test it on hard cases, run a fair test, and say what the evidence supports.

terms.meaning: A living being uses energy to build and mend their own body. They keep their inside different from the outside, and they come from other living beings.
terms.example: A neem tree, a crow and the bacteria in curd are all alive.
terms.art: A neem tree, a crow on a wall and a curd bowl, each with a small label saying alive.

terms.meaning: A meaning that scientists use for now because it is useful, even though they know it might change.
terms.example: NASA uses a working definition of life to decide what to look for on Mars.
terms.art: A scientist at a desk with a sticky note on a rover model that says 'life = ?' and a pencil with a rubber.

terms.meaning: A case that does not fit a rule.
terms.example: A mule almost never has young. She is an exception to 'living things make young'.
terms.art: A row of identical ducks with one rabbit in the middle, circled.

terms.meaning: All the chemical changes in a living body that turn food into energy and into new body parts.
terms.example: Your body breaks down rice for energy, then uses some of it to build muscle.
terms.art: A plate of rice and dal with arrows leading to a running child and to a growing muscle.

terms.meaning: A living body keeping something steady, such as warmth, even when the outside changes.
terms.example: You sweat when you are hot and shiver when you are cold, so you stay near 37 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A child sweating in the sun on one side and shivering in a blanket on the other, both with a thermometer reading 37.

terms.meaning: The thin skin around every cell. It decides what goes in and what stays out.
terms.example: The skin around each beetroot cell keeps the red colour inside until the beetroot is heated.
terms.art: A beetroot cell drawn as a round room with a thin wall and red dots inside.

terms.meaning: What is needed to make anything happen, such as heat, light or movement.
terms.example: Food gives your body energy, and petrol gives a scooter energy.
terms.art: A child eating idli beside a scooter being filled with petrol, with the same glowing arrow above each.

terms.meaning: Something that is used up to give energy.
terms.example: Wax is the fuel of a candle, and rice is fuel for your body.
terms.art: A candle with a shrinking wax pool and a child's plate of rice, each with an arrow to a small flame sign.

terms.meaning: A solid whose tiny parts are stacked in a repeating pattern.
terms.example: Salt grains are tiny cubes, and mishri, the rock sugar, is made of sugar crystals.
terms.art: A close-up of salt grains as small cubes, next to a piece of mishri on a thread.

terms.meaning: Alive but resting, with almost nothing going on.
terms.example: A dry seed in a jar is dormant until water arrives.
terms.art: A dry moong seed in a jar with a small 'zzz' beside the jar.

terms.meaning: A part that senses the temperature and switches heating or cooling on and off to keep it steady.
terms.example: The thermostat inside a fridge switches the cooling on when the inside gets too warm.
terms.art: A fridge with its door open, showing a small dial and a thermometer inside.

terms.meaning: A tiny package of instructions inside a protein coat. It can make copies only inside a living cell.
terms.example: The virus that causes a cold.
terms.art: A round virus with spikes on her coat, drawn next to a much bigger cell.

terms.meaning: Change over many generations. Young are a little different from their parents, and the differences that help them survive are passed on.
terms.example: Bacteria that survive an antibiotic have young who also survive it.
terms.art: A line of bacteria in four generations, with a few turning dark and the dark ones increasing.

terms.meaning: Keeps going and repairs itself, as long as there is food and energy, without anyone rebuilding it.
terms.example: A bacterium in curd keeps going on milk sugar. A robot needs a person to build and mend it.
terms.art: A bacterium eating at a milk-sugar table, next to a robot with a toolbox beside it.

terms.example: A money plant stem cut in two grows new roots, and a gecko can grow a new tail.
terms.art: A money plant cutting with white roots in a jar, and a gecko with a short new tail.

terms.example: A mule is almost always sterile, and most worker honeybees never lay eggs.
terms.art: A mule beside a worker honeybee, each with a small crossed-out egg.

terms.meaning: Burning. Fuel joins with oxygen from the air and gives out heat and light.
terms.example: A candle flame is combustion of wax gas.
terms.art: A candle flame with arrows for wax gas coming in and air coming in, and heat and light going out.

explanations.concept: What a definition is for: a rule that is useful, not a law of nature
explanations.definition: A working definition is a rule scientists use for now, because it is useful, even though they know it may change.
explanations.description: A definition is a rule we write so that people mean the same thing by a word. The word 'alive' was in use for thousands of years before anyone knew what cells were. So the word came first, and the science came later. Scientists now write working definitions of life. A working definition does not claim to be the truth about nature. It only has to be useful, for example for deciding what a space probe should look for. When a hard case breaks the rule, scientists do not throw the case away. They learn something from it, and they mend the rule.
examples: The seven signs of life are a working definition. They work well for crows, trees and people.
A flame breaks the seven signs, so the seven signs are not enough.
NASA's definition is another working definition, written for the search for life on other worlds.
explanations.art: A notebook page with a rule written at the top, a hard case drawn beside it, and an arrow showing the rule being rewritten.

explanations.concept: Why one sign of life is never enough: fire
explanations.definition: Combustion is burning. Fuel joins with oxygen and gives out heat and light.
explanations.description: A candle flame does many of the things on the list of life. It takes in fuel, which is wax gas. It takes in air. It gives out heat, light, carbon dioxide and water. It grows when you add more wick. It moves, and it spreads to a new wick or a dry leaf. It even goes out when it runs out of food or air. Yet a flame is not alive. A flame is a place where fuel is joining with oxygen, a burning that is happening right now. Nothing in a flame is built, kept or mended. If you blow it out, nothing is left that could start again. A flame is only as old as its fuel.
examples: A forest fire eats, breathes, grows and travels far.
A diya flame needs oil and a wick, and goes out under a katori.
A flame can light a second wick, but both flames are made of the same burning, with no instructions passed on.
explanations.art: A candle flame with arrows for wax gas and air going in, and heat, light and smoke going out.

explanations.concept: Crystals grow by adding more of the same, living things grow by turning other things into themselves
explanations.definition: Metabolism is all the chemical changes in a living body that turn food into energy and into new body parts.
explanations.description: Put a grain of salt in strong salt water and it grows. Break the crystal and each piece grows too. A crystal can even copy its pattern. Each new layer is laid down just like the one below it. But look at what the crystal is doing. It only adds more salt that was already in the water. Nothing is changed into salt. A bean sprout is different. A bean sprout is made of sugar, water, air and a little soil. None of these is a bean sprout. The sprout takes them in and changes them into new roots and leaves. This turning of other stuff into your own body is called metabolism. A crystal stacks. A living thing builds.
examples: Salt in a pan grows by stacking more salt from the sea water.
A coconut sprout turns rain, air and the nut's food into roots and leaves.
You turn rice, dal and curd into muscle, blood and bone.
explanations.art: A salt crystal getting bigger by adding tiny cubes on the outside, beside a bean sprout with arrows showing water, air and sugar turning into root and leaf.

explanations.concept: Staying different: a living body works to stay unlike its surroundings
explanations.definition: Homeostasis is a living body keeping something steady, such as its warmth, even when the outside changes.
explanations.description: Warm water in a tumbler cools down until it is as warm as the room. Then it stays that way. Left alone, everything drifts to match its surroundings. A living body does not. Your body stays near 37 degrees Celsius whether the room is warm or cool. It does this by burning food, by shivering, by sweating and by moving blood around. Inside every cell there is also a different amount of salt, sugar and water from outside the cell. A living thing is a place where the inside is kept unlike the outside. This is called homeostasis. It takes energy every second. When a living thing dies, the work stops and the inside slowly becomes the same as the outside.
examples: Your body stays near 37 degrees Celsius in a 28-degree room.
A fish keeps the salt in her blood at a steady level in river water.
A dead leaf, a dead insect and a cold cup of tea all end up at room temperature.
explanations.art: Two lines on a graph: a warm cup of water falling to room temperature, and a child's body temperature staying level.

explanations.concept: The skin of a cell: why heat makes a living beetroot bleed
explanations.definition: A cell membrane is the thin skin around a cell that controls what goes in and what stays out.
explanations.description: Every living cell has a thin skin around it, called the cell membrane. This skin is made of fat and protein. It works like a careful door. It lets some things in and out and keeps other things inside. In a beetroot cell, the red pigment is kept inside a bag in the cell. The membranes keep it there. Cold or room-temperature water does not hurt the membranes much, so a whole beetroot stays red inside and the water around it stays clear. Heat shakes the fat and protein of the skin out of their places. Holes open and the pigment leaks out. That is why boiled beetroot turns the cooking water red. A cell with a broken skin can no longer keep its inside different from the outside.
examples: Beetroot cubes in cold water stay in their colour, but cubes in very hot water turn the water red.
A boiled potato slice no longer keeps the water balance of a fresh slice.
Bacteria in curd are each wrapped in a skin that keeps their chemistry together.
explanations.art: Two beetroot cells drawn side by side. The left one has a whole skin and red dots inside. The right one has a torn skin and red dots leaking out.

explanations.concept: Exceptions that are alive: mules, worker bees and the sleepers
explanations.definition: Sterile means not able to have young.
explanations.description: Many people say that living things make young. But a mule almost never does, because the chromosomes from a horse mother and a donkey father do not pair up neatly. A worker honeybee almost never lays eggs either. The queen does that for the whole hive. Yet mules and worker bees are alive. So the test 'makes young' belongs to a kind of living thing across many generations, and not to each single body. Another exception is the sleeper. A dry seed, or a tiny animal dried to dust, may show no sign of life for years. Neither is dead. Each is dormant, alive but resting. So some tests have to be about what a living thing can do, and not what she is doing right now.
examples: A mule works hard on a farm and is alive, though she is almost always sterile.
A worker bee flies, feeds the young and builds the comb, and does not lay eggs.
A dormant seed does not move or eat, and yet sprouts when water arrives.
explanations.art: A mule pulling a cart, a worker bee on a flower and a dry seed, each with a small egg symbol crossed out or sleeping.

explanations.concept: Seeds and animals that wait: how long can life pause?
explanations.definition: Dormant means alive but resting, with almost nothing going on.
explanations.description: Some living things can pause their life. A seed dries out until almost nothing is going on inside. This is called dormancy. How long can it last? Most kitchen seeds are best within a couple of years. But a date palm seed found at Masada in Israel, about 2,000 years old, was sprouted by Elaine Solowey in 2005 and grew into a tree. In 2012, Svetlana Yashina's team in Russia grew whole plants of a flower called Silene from fruit tissue that had been frozen in Siberian ice for about 32,000 years. Tiny animals called tardigrades can dry up and wait, and one frozen for over 30 years woke up. Scientists call this deep pause cryptobiosis. The pause shows us that being alive is not the same as doing something right now.
examples: A sacred lotus seed from an old lake bed in China, about 1,300 years old, has sprouted.
A tardigrade dries into a tiny barrel and wakes when water returns.
Seed banks keep seeds dry and cold for many years.
explanations.art: A date palm seed in a museum drawer, a seedling in a pot, and a calendar page showing 2,000 years between them.

explanations.description: There is no agreed definition of life. Scientists have tried many. A group at NASA, in the 1990s, wrote: life is a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution. This is useful for planning how to look for life on other worlds. In 2002, the American biochemist Daniel Koshland listed seven pillars of life: a program of instructions, improvisation when conditions change, compartments, energy, regeneration, adaptability and seclusion, which means keeping each chemical reaction apart from the others. Each of these definitions has a hard case that bends it. In the NASA one, a single mule is not able to evolve alone, so the definition has to be about the whole kind. In the pillars, a dormant seed is not using much energy. Scientists use these definitions as tools, not as the final answer.
examples: NASA's definition has three parts: chemical, self-sustaining, and able to evolve by Darwin's rules.
Koshland's seven pillars come from his work as a biochemist.
The seven signs of life that you may know from school are another working definition.
explanations.art: Three notebook pages side by side, each with a different list of tests for life, and a candle flame, a mule and a seed placed below them.

perspectives.explanation: Life is a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution. The key point is that living things change over generations, so a kind of life can improve at surviving.
Life is seven things together: a program, improvisation, compartments, energy, regeneration, adaptability and seclusion. No one of them is enough, but a living thing shows them all.

perspectives.who: Carol Cleland, an American philosopher of science
perspectives.explanation: It is too early to write a definition. People used 'water' for thousands of years before anyone knew it was H2O. We will define life well only after we find a theory of life, perhaps by finding a second kind of life that did not start on Earth.

explanations.concept: Viruses: alive, not alive, or something in between?
explanations.description: A virus is a package of instructions in a protein coat. By itself, a virus does not take in food, grow or use energy. Inside a living cell, though, the virus takes over the cell and uses her machinery to make thousands of copies. Those copies change a little, and the changes are passed on, so viruses evolve. In 1935, Wendell Stanley made crystals of a plant virus, and the crystals still made plants sick when they were dissolved again. In 2003, scientists found a giant virus called mimivirus, big enough to see through a good light microscope. Whether viruses are alive depends on which tests you choose, and scientists honestly disagree.
examples: The virus that causes a cold makes copies inside the cells of a nose.
A tobacco mosaic virus crystal can lie in a jar for years and still infect a leaf.
A bacteriophage is a virus that infects only bacteria.
explanations.art: A virus with spikes landing on a cell, then the cell filling with many copies of the virus.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say viruses are not alive
perspectives.explanation: A virus has no cells and no energy of her own. She cannot grow or repair, and she cannot copy herself alone. She is a chemical that borrows life from cells.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say viruses are alive
perspectives.explanation: A virus has her own genes, she copies them, and she evolves by Darwin's rules. Needing a host does not make a virus lifeless, because many living things need a host to survive.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say 'alive' is the wrong question
perspectives.explanation: Life is not a switch with two settings. A virus shows some of the traits of life and not others, and it is more useful to say which ones.

explanations.concept: Could life be made of other things, and could we make it?
explanations.description: All the life we know uses carbon, water and cells, and passes instructions on in DNA or RNA. We have not yet found a second kind. Some scientists think that life on other worlds could use a different liquid, or a different material, and we need tests that would still work. In 2010, a team led by Craig Venter built a whole bacterial genome in a laboratory and put it into an empty bacterial cell, which then started to live and divide. In 2016, the same group built a very small cell with 473 genes and found that about 149 of those genes had no known job. So, even in the simplest known cell, scientists still do not know what everything does. Others make patterns in computers, such as the glider in John Conway's Game of Life, which moves and copies itself on a screen. Most scientists say these are models, not life. Nobody can yet say for sure.
examples: A cell with a lab-built genome has been made, but it was put inside a cell that already existed.
The glider in the Game of Life is a pattern that moves across a grid, not a living thing.
A space probe has to decide which tests to use before it lands.
explanations.art: A lab flask with a tiny cell inside it, and beside it a computer grid with a glider pattern moving across.

explanations.concept: Why the line is hard to draw
explanations.description: Put all these cases in a row: a rock, a crystal, a flame, a virus, a dry seed, a bacterium, an ant, a person. Each one has some of the traits of life and not others. A flame uses fuel, a crystal copies its pattern, a virus evolves, a dry seed waits, a bacterium builds and mends herself. No single trait separates the living things from the rest. Some philosophers say that this is like the word 'game'. There is no one thing that all games share, but we know games when we see them. Others say there is a real line, and that we have not yet found it. Both views are sensible, and the evidence we have does not settle it.
examples: No single trait is shared by all and only living things.
Scientists often use a bundle of traits at once.
A hard case helps us find which trait matters most.
explanations.art: A long row of cards from a rock on the left to a person on the right, with a wavy line over the middle that can't be placed.

perspectives.who: Some philosophers (following Ludwig Wittgenstein's idea of 'family resemblance')
perspectives.explanation: 'Alive' names a family of traits that usually come together. In nature they sometimes come apart, so a single sharp line may not exist.
There is a real line, which is Darwinian evolution by cells or by something like cells. The edge cases are rare and can be handled one by one.

agreed.text: No single sign of life, such as growing, moving or using fuel, separates living things from non-living things.
agreed.evidence: A flame grows, moves and uses fuel, and a dry seed does none of these, so each test gives a wrong answer for some case.

agreed.text: Every living thing we know is made of cells, or is a virus that needs cells.
agreed.evidence: Cells have been looked at in every kind of living thing, from bacteria to trees, since Robert Hooke and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek in the 1600s.

agreed.text: Living cells use energy to keep their insides different from their outsides.
agreed.evidence: Living cells hold different amounts of salt and other chemicals than their surroundings, and when a cell dies the differences fade.

agreed.text: Seeds, and some tiny animals, can pause their life for years and then start again.
agreed.evidence: A date palm seed about 2,000 years old was sprouted in 2005, and a tardigrade frozen for over 30 years woke up.

agreed.text: Living things build their bodies from other materials, while a crystal grows by adding more of the same.
agreed.evidence: A sprout lives on food stored in her seed and changes that food into new roots and leaves. A salt crystal in salt water gets bigger only by adding the salt that was already in the water.

agreed.text: There is no single definition of life that every scientist accepts.
agreed.evidence: The NASA definition, Koshland's seven pillars and the seven signs of life each have a hard case that bends them.

challenging.claim: Fire is alive, because it eats, breathes, grows and spreads.
challenging.who: Many children, and some of the oldest ideas. The Greek thinker Heraclitus, about 500 BCE, called the world an ever-living fire.
challenging.for: A flame passes many tests: it uses fuel and air, it grows, it moves and it spreads.
challenging.against: A flame builds nothing and mends nothing. It cannot keep its own warmth steady, and its new flames pass on no instructions. If the fuel stops, the flame ends, with nothing left to start again.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that fire counts as a living thing, because it does so much of what living things do.

challenging.claim: A thing that cannot have young is not alive.
challenging.who: Many people who learned 'living things reproduce' as a rule.
challenging.for: Making young is the way a kind of living thing goes on. Without it, a kind ends.
challenging.against: A mule, a worker bee and an old tree that no longer flowers are all alive. The test is about a kind over many generations, not about each single body.
challenging.context: This card is about the common rule that living things make young, and a case that breaks it.

challenging.claim: A thing that does nothing is dead.
challenging.who: Many people, and any rule that depends only on what a body is doing right now.
challenging.for: Signs of life such as moving, breathing and growing are things we can watch.
challenging.against: A dry seed, a dried tardigrade and a frozen bacterium do almost nothing and wake up again. What matters is what a body can still do.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that a living thing must always be doing something that we can see.

challenging.who: Some virologists. Some say giant viruses such as mimivirus, found in 2003, are a fourth branch of life.
challenging.for: Viruses have genes, they copy those genes, and they evolve by Darwin's rules.
challenging.against: A virus cannot use energy or make anything on her own. Without a host cell, she does nothing at all.
challenging.context: This card is about whether viruses count as living things, which scientists still argue about.

challenging.claim: Life must be made of carbon and water, in cells.
challenging.who: Many biologists, because every living thing we know is built this way. This is sometimes called carbon chauvinism.
challenging.for: Carbon makes long, flexible chains, and water lets chemicals move and meet. All known life uses them.
challenging.against: We have only studied one example of life, which began once on Earth. Other worlds may have other chemistries, and a test built only for our kind might miss them.
challenging.context: This card is about whether life elsewhere would have to be like life on Earth.

challenging.claim: A computer program or robot can be alive.
challenging.who: A few researchers in artificial life, such as people who study John Conway's Game of Life patterns.
challenging.for: A pattern in a computer can move, copy itself and change.
challenging.against: A program needs a computer built and powered by someone, and does not turn other stuff into its own body. Most scientists say these are models of life.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a copying pattern in a computer could count as a living thing.

big_questions.q: Warm water cools to match the room, and you do not. If staying different from the room is the work of being alive, what is happening to a body when she dies?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you measured, and what stopped.

big_questions.q: A dry seed in a drawer shows no sign of life for a hundred years and then sprouts. Was the seed alive all that time, or is 'alive' something that only happens when a body is doing things?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a seed can still do, and when we would call a seed dead.

big_questions.q: A fire, a crystal and a virus each have some traits of life. If a new thing were found that had all the traits of life but was made of something else, should we call it alive?
big_questions.hint: Think about which traits matter most to you, and why.

big_questions.q: A bee sees a flower as a pattern of ultraviolet. A child sees it as a pink. Are they seeing the same flower differently, or two different flowers? Would a being from another world see us as alive?
big_questions.hint: Think about the tests another being might use, and what they would measure.

big_questions.q: The water that turned the beetroot red was colourless a minute before. Where was the red before, and what kept it there?
big_questions.hint: Think about the skin around each cell.

big_questions.q: Your body replaces many of its atoms over months and years, yet you still call yourself you. What is it that stays the same, if not the atoms?
big_questions.hint: Think about a flame or a river, whose pieces change but whose pattern goes on.

big_questions.q: A cell with a lab-built genome has been made. If scientists one day build a whole cell from chemicals, who is its parent, and is it alive?
big_questions.hint: Think about which of the tests it would pass.

big_questions.q: Scientists agreed about water only after they knew it was H2O. What might we have to discover before we can agree about life?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a second kind of life, found on another world, might teach us.

story.title: Salt That Grows
story.note: A made-up story. Selvi, her mother Amudha and her grandmother Aachi are imagined. Sea salt really is made by letting sea water dry in shallow pans on the coast of Tamil Nadu, near Thoothukudi and in other places. Rain on salt that has not been covered is a real worry for salt workers, because it melts the salt back into water. A coconut really can sprout on the ground, with a shoot and roots coming out of the nut.
text: At four in the morning, the salt pans were the colour of pewter. Selvi walked behind her mother with a wooden rake on her shoulder. On either side lay the shallow squares of sea water, and they still held the last of the stars.

By noon the squares would be white. The sun took the water away, and the salt stayed behind. Selvi's mother, Amudha, would rake the salt into long ridges. The women would carry it in flat baskets to the heaps near the road. That was the whole trick of the place. Sea in, sun on, salt out.

Selvi's grandmother, Aachi, had worked the pans for fifty years, and Aachi said salt was alive. 'It grows,' she said, sitting on an upturned basket with her feet in the warm brine. 'Drop one grain in a pan, and by the evening it is the size of a lentil. Break a lump in two, and each half grows on. Salt is the sea's child, and it has children of its own.'

Selvi liked this. But at school that week her teacher had given her a list of the signs of life. Living things take in food. They grow. They make more of their own kind. 'Salt does not eat, Aachi,' she said.
'It eats the sea,' said Aachi, and she laughed, because Selvi had no answer.

All day Selvi turned it over. That afternoon she took a steel plate of the strongest brine from the last pan. She dropped in a single grain and carried the plate home in the shade. By the next morning the grain had grown a small crown of new cubes. Selvi looked at it with her mother's magnifying glass. Every new cube was exactly like the old one. White, square, stacked on the same corners. There was nothing in that plate but salt and water, and the salt had simply picked up more salt.
'It just stacks,' she said to herself. 'Like putting one brick on another.'

That afternoon, a wind came from the east that smelled of wet tin. Amudha looked at the sky and said one word, and every woman on the pans began to run. Rain in the dry season was the thing they feared most. The heaps by the road were piled with a month of work, and rain would melt them back to water.

Selvi ran with the rest. They dragged the big palm-leaf mats over the heaps, and they weighed them down with stones. The first fat drops hit the pans like thrown pebbles. Aachi, who could not run any more, stood at the end of the dyke and called out the order of the heaps. One heap at the far end was never covered. It was too far and the rain came too fast.

The rain fell for an hour. When it stopped, the pans were silver sheets, and the uncovered heap was a grey puddle. Aachi stood looking at it for a long time. 'My salt,' she said quietly. 'Gone back to the sea.'

Next morning, Selvi walked out along the dyke to see what was left. By the side of the track lay a coconut that had fallen there months before. A week ago she had seen a pale shoot, as fat as her finger, poking out of one eye of the nut, and a few thin roots creeping into the mud. Now, after the rain, the shoot was a hand longer. And it was green.
Selvi crouched down beside it and stayed there until the sun was hot on her back.

The same rain had fallen on both. It had melted the salt, and the salt had gone into the water and stayed there as salt. The sea had taken back exactly what it had given. But the coconut had drunk the same rain, and the water had not stayed water. It had gone into a shoot. Nothing in that shoot was coconut water, or air, or the white flesh of the nut. Yet the shoot was made of all three. The salt had only added to itself. The coconut was making herself out of things that were not herself.
She ran back to the heaps. Aachi was sitting on her basket with her feet in the brine, which was already a little thicker as the sun came back.
'The salt grows,' Selvi said, out of breath. 'But it only grows with more salt. The coconut grows out of water and air and her own nut, none of which is coconut. That is the difference.'
Aachi was quiet. Then she lifted one hand from the brine and held it up in front of her face, thin and brown and creased with fifty years of sun.

'Fifty years of rice and fish and kanji,' she said slowly. 'And not one grain of it is still rice.' She laughed until she coughed. 'So I am a very old pile of rice porridge, and the salt in my tears is salt from these very pans, and it is still salt.'
'The salt just passes through you,' said Selvi. 'It does not turn into you.'
'Then perhaps,' said Aachi, 'someone will find a salt that does.' And she winked, and went back to watching the sun take the water out of the pan.
story.epiphany: A salt crystal grows by adding more salt that was already in the water. A coconut sprout grows by turning water, air and the nut's food into roots and leaves that are none of those things. Living things build their own bodies out of other stuff.
ask: A salt crystal in strong salt water gets bigger. A sprout in a pot gets bigger. How is the way each one gets bigger different?
Salt can pass through a person's body and come out as salt. Rice cannot. What does that tell you about what happens to the rice?
What would you have to see happen, to be sure that a crystal was making itself out of other things?
