roots.context: We have tested rules for life and watched what heat does to a living cell. Now we ask what these tests tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A living thing is a place that stays different from its surroundings. Warm water cooled to match the room, but your body stayed warm. A beetroot cell kept its red inside, until heat broke the skin around it. Staying different takes work every second, and dying is when the work stops.
deep_truth.habit: We think 'alive' means having something extra, or doing one special thing such as moving or growing. But a flame does those things, and a sleeping seed does not. What living things share is ongoing work, to keep an inside that is unlike the outside.
deep_truth.evidence: In the warmth test, the warm water cooled towards the temperature of the room, but a child's own temperature stayed almost the same. In the beetroot test, cubes in cold water kept their colour, and cubes in very hot water turned the water red. If your results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: You are not only a thing, you are also a doing. Every second, your body burns food to stay warm, to rebuild itself and to keep the inside of each cell apart from the outside.
three.what_is_life: Life is the work of keeping an inside that is different from the outside, and of building that inside out of whatever the outside provides.
three.what_is_this_world: Sunlight goes into plants, plants become food, food becomes warmth, and the warmth leaves into space. Life is one of the places where this flow of energy stops for a while and builds something.

roots.thread: From the One come particles, stars, and then, on at least one world, living bodies. Everything is conscious, down to the smallest particle, and in a living body this shows up as sensing, choosing and mending. A bacterium senses food and swims towards food, and a root chooses where to grow. The edge of a living body is not a wall that cuts her off from the world. It is a boundary that she keeps rebuilding, from the world's own rice, water and air.

teachings.teaching: The Upanishad says that beings are born from food, live by food, and in the end return to food.
teachings.link: A sprout, a coconut palm and a child all build their bodies from what they take in, and one day their bodies become food and soil for others.

teachings.teaching: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker of about 500 BCE, said that the world has always been an ever-living fire, kindling in measures and going out in measures.
teachings.link: A flame keeps its shape while its fuel keeps changing. A living body does this too, and she also rebuilds herself while she does it.

teachings.source: The Questions of King Milinda (Milindapanha), the chariot passage
teachings.teaching: In this old Buddhist text, the monk Nagasena tells the king that 'chariot' is a name for the pole, the axle, the wheels and the rest put together. There is no chariot apart from the parts.
teachings.link: 'Alive' may be like 'chariot', a name for a bundle of traits that come together, such as energy use, a skin, repair and copying. No single trait is the aliveness.

science.text: Living cells use energy to keep different amounts of salt and other chemicals inside than outside. When a cell dies, the difference fades.
Nobody has an agreed definition of life. Whether life is one kind of thing with a real edge, or a bundle of traits with blurred edges, is still argued.

other_view.who: Many biologists who use the NASA definition
other_view.view: There is a real line, and it is Darwinian evolution. A living thing belongs to a line of copies that can change over generations. Keeping warm or keeping a skin is useful, but a fridge does something like it too. Evolution is the test that no flame or fridge has passed.

practice.title: Find your own warmth
practice.say: Sit still and hold one palm close to your mouth. Breathe out slowly on your palm and feel the warmth. Do this three times. Now put the same hand on your chest. Feel it rise and fall, and feel your heartbeat. Ask yourself what is working right now, without your asking.
practice.kid: Hold your palm near your mouth. Breathe out slowly on it. Feel the warmth. Do it three times. Now put your hand on your chest. Feel it rise and your heart beat.

ask: Is your warmth something you have, or something you are doing?
If a thing can stay different from its surroundings without working at it, would you call it alive?
A flame, a fridge and a bacterium each hold an inside different from the outside. What else would you need to see before you called one of them alive?
roots.art: A child holding a glass of warm water and a thermometer reading 37, with a faint line of heat rising from their chest into the room.

games.title: Fool the Test: does the test give the right answer?
games.context: In this card game, each card names a thing and a test for life. You decide if the thing passes the test. Then you find out if the test gave the right answer about whether the thing is alive.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile in the middle of a table, with a Passes token and a Fails token in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One player reading a card aloud while the others put a token face down in front of them.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a token.

setup.art: Tokens turned over together, and the reader showing the back of the card with the answer.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader shows the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a thing and a test on the front, the answer on the back

items.f: A candle flame. Test: does it grow?
items.b: Passes. A flame gets bigger when you add more wick. A flame is not alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A candle flame. Test: does it use up food and air?
items.b: Passes. A flame uses up wax gas and air. A flame is not alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A candle flame. Test: can it spread to make more of itself?
items.b: Passes. A flame can light a new wick. A flame is not alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A salt crystal in strong salt water. Test: does it grow?
items.b: Passes. More salt from the water joins the crystal. A crystal is not alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A broken piece of a salt crystal. Test: can each piece keep growing on its own?
items.b: Passes. Each piece grows in strong salt water. A crystal is not alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A mule. Test: does she make young?
items.b: Fails. A mule is almost always sterile. A mule is alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A worker honeybee. Test: does she lay eggs?
items.b: Fails. A worker bee almost never lays eggs. The queen does. A worker bee is alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A dry moong seed in a jar. Test: does it move?
items.b: Fails. A dry seed does not move. A seed is alive and resting, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A dry moong seed in a jar. Test: does it use food and air?
items.b: Fails, almost. A resting seed uses almost nothing. A seed is alive and resting, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A date palm seed, 2,000 years old, in a drawer. Test: does it show any sign of life while it waits?
items.b: Fails. It showed no sign for 2,000 years, then sprouted in 2005. It was alive and resting, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A robot vacuum cleaner. Test: does it move around and sense walls?
items.b: Passes. It moves and senses. A robot is not alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A robot vacuum cleaner. Test: does it mend itself when a wheel breaks?
items.b: Fails. Someone has to repair it. A robot is not alive, so this test is fair.

items.f: A fridge. Test: does it keep its inside different from the outside?
items.b: Passes. A fridge keeps its inside cold. A fridge is not alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A child's body in a cool room. Test: does it stay near 37 degrees Celsius?
items.b: Passes. A body burns food to stay warm. A child is alive, so this test is fair.

items.f: A gecko on a cold morning. Test: is she warmer than the wall?
items.b: Fails. A gecko matches her surroundings. A gecko is alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A tumbler of warm water. Test: does it stay warm for an hour by itself?
items.b: Fails. The water cools to match the room. Water is not alive, so this test is fair.

items.f: A raw beetroot cube in cold water. Test: does the red stay inside the cells?
items.b: Passes. The cell skins hold the red inside. The cells are alive, so this test is fair.

items.f: A beetroot cube after boiling. Test: does the red stay inside the cells?
items.b: Fails. Heat breaks the cell skins. The cells are dead, so this test is fair.

items.f: A cold virus. Test: can it make copies of itself on its own?
items.b: Fails. A virus needs a living cell to copy. Whether a virus is alive is debated, so scientists disagree if this test is fair.

items.f: A bacterium in curd. Test: does she have a skin around her inside?
items.b: Passes. A bacterium has a cell membrane. A bacterium is alive, so this test is fair.

items.f: A forest fire. Test: does it move across the land?
items.b: Passes. A fire can spread fast. A fire is not alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A cloud. Test: does it grow?
items.b: Passes. A cloud can get bigger as water gathers in it. A cloud is not alive, so this test is fooled.

items.f: A tardigrade dried to a tiny barrel. Test: does she use energy?
items.b: Fails, almost. A dried tardigrade uses almost none. She wakes when water returns, so she is alive and this test is fooled.

items.f: A neem tree with a cut branch. Test: can the tree grow the branch back?
items.b: Passes. Trees regrow from the cut. A neem tree is alive, so this test is fair.

printables.title: 8 tokens: four that say Passes and four that say Fails

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down: Passes or Fails. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the first word of the back scores one point.
The reader then says if the test was fooled or fair. Before the reveal, each player says aloud "fooled" or "fair" as they turn their token. A player who was right scores one more point.
After each card, the reader writes F on a score sheet if the test was fooled, and a tick if it was fair. The reader's job passes to the player on the left.
If you play alone, you are every player. Guess, then read the back, and score one point for each right guess. You win if you score 30 or more out of 48.
The game ends when all 24 cards are read. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win. Count the F marks too, to see how often tests are fooled.

flow.do: Print and cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. No printer? Copy each card onto a paper slip. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player a Passes and a Fails token.
flow.say: Each card names a thing and a test for life. You decide if the thing passes the test or fails it. Then we find out if the test gave the right answer.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take a Passes and a Fails token.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fool the Test. It is a card game about tests for life. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play the first three cards. The reader reads the front. Every other player puts one token face down. Turn the tokens over together. The reader reads the back.
flow.say: Read the front aloud. Everyone picks Passes or Fails, face down. Turn the tokens over together. Then the reader reads the back.
flow.kid: Read a card. Pick a token. Turn the tokens over. Read the back.
flow.parent: After the first reveal, ask your child what they notice. Keep the first rounds slow, so everyone sees how a round works. Two players is enough: one reads and one guesses, and then swap. For three or four, the readers take turns.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first three cards and learn how a round works.

flow.do: Keep playing until all 24 cards are read. After each card, say if the test was fooled or fair. Write F or a tick on the score sheet.
flow.say: Keep going. After each card, the reader says: fooled, or fair? Write down an F for fooled and a tick for fair.
flow.kid: Keep playing. After each card, say fooled or fair. Write F or a tick.

ask.q: Why did that test give a wrong answer?
good: Because a flame also does it.
Because the thing is an exception.

flow.parent: A test is fooled when it gives the wrong answer about whether something is alive. A thing that passes but is not alive fools the test. A thing that fails but is alive fools it too.

check.q: A test says a mule is not alive because she makes no young. Is the test fooled or fair?
options: Fooled, because a mule is alive
Fair, because mules make no young
It cannot be said
check.why: A mule is alive. A test that says she is not alive gives the wrong answer, so it is fooled.

flow.context: In this step, you play the rest of the cards and keep score.

flow.do: Count how many cards were fooled and how many were fair. Ask your child what they notice about the fooled cards. Then add up the scores.
flow.say: Count the F marks. How many tests were fooled? Which things fooled the tests most often? What do you notice?
flow.kid: Count the F marks. Which things fooled the tests most? What do you notice?
flow.parent: Flames, crystals, seeds, mules and robots fool the tests most. After your child has said what they notice, explain: that is why scientists use a bundle of tests together, and why they still argue about the hard cases.
flow.think: If most simple tests are fooled by something, what could you do to find out if something is alive?
flow.context: In this step, you look for the pattern in the fooled tests.

experiments.title: Beetroot Bleed: what does heat do to the skin of a living cell?
experiments.question: A raw beetroot keeps its red colour inside its cells. At what water temperature does the colour start to leak out?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Four glasses of water, from icy cold to very hot, will each get beetroot cubes. Which glass will turn the reddest, and which will stay the clearest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every glass has the same amount of water, the same number of cubes cut to the same size, the same rinse and the same waiting time. Only the water temperature changes, so any difference in colour comes from the temperature. The cold glass is the control. It shows what whole, unheated cells do.

materials.item: 1 raw beetroot (chukandar), washed
a knife and a chopping board, used by a grown-up
4 clear glasses
a measuring cup or a katori for half a cup of water
a kettle, and a jug of tap water
cold water from the fridge
a sheet of white paper
a clock or phone timer
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the beetroot and pours the hot water. Keep children away from the kettle. Pour the just-boiled water into a thick glass or a steel tumbler, or let the kettle rest for one minute first, because thin glass can crack. Beetroot stains hands and clothes, so wear an old shirt.
experiments.record: For each glass, write a colour score at 5 minutes and at 20 minutes. Zero is clear water and four is deep red. Then draw a bar for each glass, using the 20-minute score.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you put beetroot cubes in water of four different temperatures and watch how much red leaks out. You find out what heat does to the cells.

setup.art: A raw beetroot being cut by a grown-up into small cubes on a chopping board, with eight cubes in a row.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts eight cubes, each about one centimetre wide.

setup.art: Eight beetroot cubes in a sieve under a running tap, with the red juice running away.
setup.caption: 2. Rinse the cubes under the tap for one minute.

setup.art: Four clear glasses labelled A, B, C and D in a row on white paper, with a jug, a fridge bottle and a kettle behind them.
setup.caption: 3. Half a cup of water in each glass: cold, room, hand-hot and very hot.

setup.art: Two beetroot cubes being dropped into each glass at the same moment, with a timer on the table.
setup.caption: 4. Drop two cubes into each glass at the same moment.

setup.art: Four glasses side by side, with water from clear to deep red, and a score card from zero to four.
setup.caption: 5. Look at the colour after 5 minutes and after 20 minutes. Give each glass a score.

flow.do: Show your child the beetroot and the four glasses. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will put beetroot cubes in four glasses of water, from icy to very hot. Which glass will turn the reddest? Which will stay clearest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four glasses of water, from cold to hot. Which one turns reddest? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that glass will turn the reddest?
good: The red is stuck inside and heat lets it out.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write it down so your child can compare it later. Two or more children: each child makes their own guess, then one child pours with the grown-up, one starts the timer and one scores. Swap jobs for the 20-minute look, and score the glasses separately before comparing. With one child, the grown-up only pours the hot water.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Beetroot Bleed test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts eight cubes from a raw beetroot, each about one centimetre wide. Rinse the cubes under the tap for one minute.
flow.say: A knife breaks the cells on the cut faces, and red juice leaks out. Rinse the cubes until the water runs nearly clear. Then any red we see later comes from whole cells.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts eight small cubes. Rinse them under the tap for one minute.
flow.parent: Cubes about one centimetre wide are best. If they are very small, much of the red leaks at once from cut cells. Pat the cubes dry on a tissue before dropping them in.

check.q: Why do we rinse the cubes before the test?
options: The cut cells leaked juice, and rinsing washes it off so we only see red from whole cells
To make the cubes taste better
To make the beetroot colder
check.why: The knife breaks some cells, and they leak. If we did not rinse, every glass would be pink from the start and we could not tell what the water temperature did.

flow.context: In this step, you cut the beetroot and rinse the cubes so that the test is fair.

flow.do: Label four glasses A, B, C and D. Pour half a cup of water into each. A is cold from the fridge. B is tap water at room temperature. C is hand-hot, from a kettle mixed with tap water. D is very hot, from a just-boiled kettle.
flow.say: A grown-up pours the hot water. A is cold, B is room water, C is as warm as a bath, and D is very hot. Each has the same amount.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours the water. A is cold. B is room water. C is warm. D is very hot.
flow.parent: C should feel comfortably hot on the back of the wrist, roughly 50 degrees Celsius, so about half boiled water and half tap water. D is hot enough to hurt, so keep your child's hands away. Put the white paper behind the glasses so the colours are easy to see. Use a thick glass or steel tumbler for D. Use the same cup to measure the water for every glass.

check.q: Why do all four glasses get the same amount of water and the same number of cubes?
options: So only the temperature changes
So the glasses look neat
So the water does not spill
check.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If one glass had more water, we would not know if the temperature or the amount of water made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you set up four glasses with the same water, at four temperatures.

flow.do: Drop two cubes into each glass at the same moment. Start the timer. At 5 minutes and again at 20 minutes, look at each glass. Score each glass from 0 to 4. Zero is clear water. Four is deep red.
flow.say: Drop the cubes in all together. Watch the water. After 5 minutes, give each glass a score. Look again at 20 minutes. Which glass changed the most?
flow.kid: Drop two cubes in each glass. Watch for 20 minutes. Give each glass a score from zero to four.

ask.q: What do you notice in each glass?
good: The hot one went red fast.
The warm one went a little pink.

flow.parent: Hold the white paper behind each glass to judge the colour. Typical results, which can vary with the beetroot, are glass A and B clear to very pale pink, glass C light pink, and glass D pink to deep red within minutes. Beetroot is cheap (a kilo is about Rs 40), so if the result is unclear, repeat with fresh cubes. If every glass looks the same, your cubes were too small or not rinsed enough. Start again with bigger cubes and fresh water.

check.q: Glass A stays clear and glass D turns deep red. What does this suggest?
options: Heat damages whatever kept the red colour inside the cells
Beetroot likes hot water
Cold water makes the colour disappear
check.why: The cold glass shows the colour stays inside whole cells. The hot glass shows that heat lets it out. The skin around each cell is what changed.

flow.context: In this step, you put the beetroot in and watch the colour change.

flow.do: Draw a bar for each glass, using the 20-minute score. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each glass. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the red is kept inside each cell, and that heat damaged the skin around the cell so the red leaked out. After they have said what they saw, explain: every cell has a thin skin, called the cell membrane, made of fat and protein. Heat shakes it out of shape, and holes open. A living cell keeps its inside different from the outside, and a heated cell cannot.
flow.think: Boiled beetroot turns the cooking water red. Now you know why. What had happened to the cells?
flow.context: In this step, you look at your results and say what they show.

experiments.title: Staying Warm: who keeps their own temperature?
experiments.question: After half an hour in the same room, which stays warm: a tumbler of warm water, a bottle of warm water wrapped in a thick sock, or you?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Over half an hour, which will cool down the most, and which will cool down the least? Do you think your own temperature will change? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The tumbler and the bottle are filled from the same jug of warm water at the same time, and all three sit in the same room. You measure them at the same times, using the same thermometer. Only what is being measured changes: open water, wrapped water and a living child. The open tumbler is the control.

materials.item: a digital thermometer of the kind used for fever (many homes have one), covered with cling film or a tissue when it goes in water
a steel tumbler holding about one cup of water
a small plastic or steel bottle with a screw cap, filled with the same amount of water as the tumbler
a thick woollen sock or a small towel, and a rubber band
a jug of warm water, about as warm as a bath and no hotter than 42 degrees Celsius
a tissue or a little cling film for the thermometer
a clock or phone timer
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Never use a glass thermometer with silver liquid. Use water no hotter than a warm bath, about 42 degrees Celsius at most. A grown-up pours the warm water. Wipe the thermometer tip with a clean tissue between uses, and wash it with soap and water at the end. If the thermometer is used for water and for the armpit, put cling film over the tip for the water, and use a new piece each time. If several children take turns, wash the tip with soap and water between children.
experiments.record: Write the temperature of the tumbler and the bottle every 5 minutes for 30 minutes. Write your child's temperature at the start, at 15 minutes and at 30 minutes. Then draw one line for each.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you watch warm water and a child sit in the same room for half an hour. You find out which one stays warm by itself.

setup.art: A child sitting on a stool with a digital thermometer under one arm and a clock beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Measure your own temperature under your arm. Write it down.

setup.art: A steel tumbler and a small bottle, both filled from the same jug of warm water, with the bottle wrapped in a thick sock.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the tumbler and the bottle from the same jug. Wrap the bottle in a sock.

setup.art: A thermometer in the tumbler of water, a clock beside it, and the results table being filled in.
setup.caption: 3. Every 5 minutes, measure the tumbler and the bottle and write the numbers.

setup.art: The child still sitting quietly with the thermometer under one arm at the end of half an hour.
setup.caption: 4. At 15 and 30 minutes, measure your own temperature again.

setup.art: A line graph with three lines: a falling one for the tumbler, a slower falling one for the bottle and a flat one for the child.
setup.caption: 5. Draw one line for each. Compare them.

flow.do: Show your child the tumbler, the wrapped bottle and the thermometer. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will watch warm water and you for half an hour in the same room. Who will cool the most? Who will cool the least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Warm water in a tumbler. Warm water in a wrapped bottle. And you. Who cools most? Why?

ask.q: Do you think your temperature will go down, up, or stay about the same? Why?
good: It will stay the same because I am alive.
It will go down like the water.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Staying Warm test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Sit your child down quietly. Wipe the thermometer tip. Put it under one armpit with the arm pressed down. Wait for the beep. Write the number as time zero.
flow.say: Sit quietly and press your arm down on the thermometer. Wait for the beep. This is your starting temperature.
flow.kid: Sit still. Put the thermometer under your arm. Press down. Wait for the beep.
flow.parent: A normal temperature under the arm is about 36 to 37 degrees Celsius. Children are often a little warmer after running about, so let your child sit for five minutes first.
flow.context: In this step, you measure your own temperature before the test starts.

flow.do: A grown-up pours warm water from one jug into the tumbler and into the bottle. Screw the cap on the bottle and wrap it in the sock. Measure both and write the starting numbers.
flow.say: Warm water goes into both from the same jug, so they start the same. The sock goes round the bottle. Measure each one and write the numbers.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours warm water in both. Wrap the bottle in a sock. Measure both.
flow.parent: The water should be about 40 to 42 degrees Celsius, as warm as a comfortable bath. To measure the bottle, open the cap, put the thermometer tip in, then close the cap again and keep it wrapped. Wrap the thermometer tip in cling film if it is not made for water.

check.q: Why do we fill the tumbler and the bottle from the same jug at the same time?
options: So both start at the same temperature
So the water tastes the same
So the bottle is heavier
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the water in one started hotter, we could not tell if the sock or the starting temperature made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the warm water and measure where it starts.

flow.do: At 5, 10 and 15 minutes, measure the tumbler and the bottle and write the numbers. At 15 minutes, measure your child under the arm too.
flow.say: Measure the tumbler and the bottle every five minutes. At 15 minutes, measure yourself too. Sit quietly in between.
flow.kid: Measure the tumbler and the bottle every five minutes. At 15 minutes, measure yourself.
flow.parent: Keep the room still, away from a fan pointing at the tumbler. Your child must sit still and not run about, because exercise warms the body. Measure the bottle quickly and screw the cap back on, so little heat escapes. Armpit readings can wobble by a few tenths of a degree, so take the same reading twice if it looks odd. With two or more children: one is the body being measured, one reads the tumbler, one the bottle, one writes. Swap roles if the thermometer is shared, and the second child can be measured at the end for a comparison.
flow.context: In this step, you take the first readings while the water cools.

flow.do: At 20, 25 and 30 minutes, measure the tumbler and the bottle and write the numbers. At 30 minutes, measure your child under the arm again.
flow.say: Keep measuring every five minutes. At 30 minutes, measure yourself one last time. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Keep measuring every five minutes. At 30 minutes, measure yourself again.

ask.q: What do you notice about the three sets of numbers?
good: The sock bottle went down more slowly.
My number stayed about the same.

flow.parent: Typical results, which vary with the room and the size of the tumbler, in a room near 28 to 30 degrees Celsius are the tumbler falling by roughly 4 to 8 degrees, the wrapped bottle falling by roughly 2 to 4 degrees, and the child changing by half a degree or less. In a very hot room the water falls less. If the wrapped bottle and the tumbler fall by almost the same amount, check that the sock is thick and the bottle is closed. Move to the coolest room, because the test needs a room cooler than your body.

check.q: Imagine the water went from 41 to 34 degrees, and the child went from 36.6 to 36.7 degrees. What does this show?
options: The water drifted towards the room's temperature, and the child's body worked to stay warm
The thermometer was broken
The child was cold and the water was alive
check.why: Left alone, warm water cools until it matches the room. A living body burns food to stay warm, so it did not drift.

flow.context: In this step, you take the last readings and see where each one ended up.

flow.do: Draw one line for each on the same graph. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then ask the last question.
flow.say: Draw three lines. Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says the water drifted towards the room's warmth, the sock slowed the drift but did not stop it, and the child stayed steady. After they have said what they saw, explain: a living body burns food to make heat, and uses sweat, shivering and blood flow to keep steady. A gecko, a frog, a fish and a plant mostly match their surroundings, and they are alive. So 'stays warmer than the room' is a test that works for birds and mammals, and gives the wrong answer for many living things. Cold-blooded animals still use energy every second to keep other things steady inside their cells.
flow.think: A gecko on a cold morning is as cold as the wall. If you measured her, what would the thermometer say? Would you call her not alive?
flow.context: In this step, you look at the lines and say what they show.

experiments.title: Waking Up: do older seeds sprout less often?
experiments.question: Seeds can wait a long time. Does a seed that has waited longer sprout less often, and how much less?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. You will have groups of seeds of different ages. Which group will have the most sprouts, and how many out of 10 will sprout in the oldest group? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every group has the same kind of whole seed, the same number of seeds, the same plate, the same damp tissue and the same place and time. Only the age of the seeds changes. The youngest seeds are the control. Use the date on the packet for the age.

materials.item: whole seeds of one kind, such as whole green moong (the quickest and most reliable) or methi, from 3 or 4 packets or jars of different ages, with the date written on each. A packet bought today counts as the youngest. If you cannot find different ages, use a fresh packet, the oldest packet you have, and ten seeds boiled for 5 minutes by a grown-up as a dead group
4 plates or lids, and 4 more plates to cover them in hot weather
kitchen tissue paper
water in a cup
a marker
a small magnifying glass, if you have one
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Whole seeds are a choking risk for children under five. Throw away any seeds with mould, and do not eat the seeds from this test. A grown-up does the boiling. Wash your hands after touching damp seeds.
experiments.record: Count the sprouts in each group on day 3 and day 4. Then draw a bar for each group.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you wake up seeds of different ages and count how many sprout. You find out if a seed that has waited longer is as ready to wake.

setup.art: Four packets and jars of whole seeds in a row, each with a date written on a label, and a marker beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Find seeds of different ages. Write the date of each on its label.

setup.art: A plate with damp tissue paper and ten seeds spread out on it, with a label beside the plate.
setup.caption: 2. Put ten seeds from each packet on damp tissue on its own plate.

setup.art: Four plates in a row on a shelf in the shade, each with its label.
setup.caption: 3. Keep the plates in the same place. Keep the tissue damp.

setup.art: A child counting small green sprouts on a plate with a magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 4. On day 3 and day 4, count the sprouts on each plate.

setup.art: A bar chart with one bar for each age, the tallest bar for the youngest seeds.
setup.caption: 5. Draw a bar for each group.

flow.do: Find whole seeds of the same kind in 3 or 4 packets or jars of different ages. Write the date on a label for each. Ask your child for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Look through the kitchen for the same kind of whole seed, bought at different times. Write the date on each label. Which will sprout best? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find seeds of the same kind from different times. Label each. Which will sprout best? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the oldest seeds will do worst?
good: They have been waiting too long.
They have used up their food.

flow.parent: Use whole seeds, never split dal, because split dal cannot sprout. If you only have one packet, borrow seeds from a neighbour or buy a fresh packet of the same kind. Some shop seeds are heated or treated, so a group may not sprout at all. That is a result too. Write down what you find. Kitchen moong kept sealed and dry often still sprouts well after two or three years, so the groups may look almost the same. That is an honest result: say it, and say which groups were not very old. A boiled group will not sprout and shows what a dead seed does. Two or more children: each child looks after one or two plates and counts them, then everyone compares.

check.q: Why do all four groups use the same kind of seed?
options: So only the age changes
So the plates look the same
So the seeds are the same size
check.why: If one group were moong and another chana, we would not know whether the age or the kind of seed made the difference.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Waking Up test. You collect the seeds and guess before you test.

flow.do: Wet the tissue and lay it on each plate. Count out ten seeds from the first packet onto the first plate. Do the same for each packet. Label each plate.
flow.say: Wet the tissue so it is damp but not dripping. Put ten seeds on each plate, spread out. Check each plate has the right label.
flow.kid: Wet the tissue. Put ten seeds on each plate. Label each plate.
flow.parent: Damp, not soaking. Seeds that sit in water can rot instead of sprouting. Keep the plates in the shade, in the same place, and away from the fridge. Rewet the tissue each day if it dries. In hot weather above about 35 degrees Celsius, cover each plate with another plate to stop the tissue drying out, and lift it once a day to let air in. Moong sprouts in 1 to 2 days in warm weather, so do not worry if some are well up by day 3. Count them anyway.
flow.context: In this step, you set up one plate for each age of seed.

flow.do: Look at the plates. Count the sprouts on each plate and write the number in the table. Keep the tissue damp.
flow.say: Look at each plate. A sprout is a seed with a small white root. Count them and write the numbers. Put the plates back.
flow.kid: Count the sprouts on each plate. Write the numbers. Keep the tissue damp.
flow.parent: A sprout means a small white root, at least as long as the seed is wide. Do not remove sprouts from the plate.
flow.context: In this step, you count the first sprouts, two days after you set up.

flow.do: Count the sprouts on each plate again. Write the numbers. Draw a bar for each group.
flow.say: Count the sprouts again. Draw a bar for each group. Which group did best? Which did worst?
flow.kid: Count again. Draw a bar for each group. Which did best?

check.q: The youngest seeds sprouted 9 out of 10 and the oldest only 2 out of 10. What is the best claim?
options: In this test, the older seeds sprouted less often
All old seeds are dead
Young seeds are cleverer
check.why: A claim should stick to what the test showed. The test only shows that these older seeds sprouted less often. It does not say that every old seed is dead, because even the oldest group had two sprouts.

flow.context: In this step, you count again, and then draw your results.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then ask the last question.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that more of the older seeds did not wake, that a few did, and that the seeds are alive but resting. After they have said what they saw, explain: a dormant seed uses almost no energy, but the seed's tiny store of repair work still runs, and over time damage builds up inside the seed. In the right conditions, such as very dry and cool, damage builds up slowly. The 2,000-year-old date palm seed was kept dry in a dry place. Most kitchen seeds are kept in warm, humid kitchens, so they lose their ability to wake much faster.
flow.think: A date palm seed about 2,000 years old sprouted. How could one seed wait so long when your old seeds did worse?
flow.context: In this step, you say what the evidence shows.

schedule.what: Find seeds of different ages, guess, and set up the plates.
Count the sprouts on each plate. Keep the tissue damp.
Count again, draw the bars, and say what the evidence shows.

activities.title: Break Your Own Rule: write a test for life and fool it

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
the list of eight cases in the steps

schedule.what: Write a rule for life. Test it on eight cases. Mend it and test again.

activities.record: A table with eight rows, one for each case. In each row write what your rule says, what is really true, and whether they match. Then write your rule before and after you mended it.
activities.context: In this activity, you write your own rule for what is alive and then try to break it with eight hard cases. Scientists do exactly this.

setup.art: A sheet of paper headed 'Something is alive if it...' with a child writing a rule under it.
setup.caption: 1. Write your rule for life.

setup.art: A table with eight rows for the cases and three columns: my rule says, really is, match.
setup.caption: 2. Test the rule on eight cases and fill in the table.

setup.art: The same sheet with the rule crossed out and a new, longer rule written beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Mend the rule and test it again.

flow.do: Give your child a sheet of paper and a pencil. Ask them to finish the sentence 'Something is alive if it...'. Write their rule at the top.
flow.say: Finish this sentence in your own words. 'Something is alive if it...'. Write the rule you think is best.
flow.kid: Finish this sentence. Something is alive if it... Write your best rule.

ask.q: Why did you pick that rule?
good: Because living things always do it.
Because it is what animals do.
Because it is what my teacher said.

flow.parent: Take any rule they give. Common rules are 'it moves', 'it grows', 'it eats', 'it breathes' or 'it has babies'. Write the rule exactly as they say it. Two to four children: each child writes their own rule in secret, then everyone tests all the rules on the same eight cases. The rule that gets the most cases right wins, and then mend it together. With one child, you can also write a rule and try to break it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Break Your Own Rule. You write a rule for life.

flow.do: Read the eight cases one at a time. The cases are a candle flame, a salt crystal growing in brine, a mule and a dry seed in a jar. The rest are a worker bee, a robot vacuum cleaner, a virus and a person asleep. For each, ask what the rule says. Then say what is really true.
flow.say: Here are eight cases. For each one, use your rule to say alive or not alive. Then I will tell you what scientists say. Do they match?
flow.kid: Use your rule on each case. Alive or not alive? Then check if you were right.

ask.q: Which case was the hardest for your rule?

flow.parent: What is really true: the flame is not alive. It uses fuel and air, grows and spreads. The salt crystal is not alive. It grows by adding salt from the brine. The mule is alive, though almost never able to have young. The dry seed is alive but resting. The worker bee is alive, though workers almost never lay eggs. The robot vacuum cleaner is not alive. It moves and senses, but someone built it and charges it. A virus is debated. It copies and evolves, but only inside a living cell. The sleeping person is alive. Count how many cases the rule got right.

check.q: Your rule says 'alive means it moves'. A dry seed does not move, but is alive. What does this show?
options: The rule has an exception, so it needs mending
The seed is not alive
Rules about life are never any use
check.why: A single case that breaks a rule shows the rule is not complete. Scientists then mend the rule and test again, which is what you will do next.

flow.context: In this step, you test your rule on eight hard cases.

flow.do: Ask your child to change one word, or add one part, to mend the rule. Test the new rule on the same eight cases. Count how many it gets right now.
flow.say: Change your rule so it gets more cases right. You can add a word or a part. Then try all eight cases again.
flow.kid: Mend your rule. Test it on the eight cases again. Count the right answers.
flow.parent: A good mended rule is often longer, such as 'it uses fuel and can make young'. Notice that no simple rule will get all eight right, and that is the point. Many of the cases are exceptions to every simple rule.
flow.context: In this step, you mend your rule and test it again.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Ask if any rule could get every case right.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think your rule would do? What happened? Why do you think the rule got some wrong?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what happened, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says the rule got some cases wrong, that the hard cases were the flame, the seed and the mule, and that you can mend a rule by adding to it. After they have said it, explain: scientists have the same trouble. Every simple test for life has an exception, so they use a bundle of tests together.
flow.think: Could any rule get all eight cases right? What would it need to say?
flow.context: In this step, you say what your testing showed.

activities.title: Three Tests, Eight Cases: what scientists' definitions say

materials.item: a sheet of paper, a ruler and a pencil

schedule.what: Draw a table of three tests and eight cases. Fill it in and look for disagreements.

activities.record: A table with eight rows and three columns. In each box write yes, no or maybe. Then circle the cases where the three tests disagree.
activities.context: In this activity, you use three real definitions of life on eight cases, and you find where the tests disagree.

setup.art: A table with three columns headed The seven signs, NASA's test and Koshland's pillars, and eight rows of cases.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with three tests across the top and eight cases down the side.

setup.art: A child writing yes, no or maybe in the boxes of the table with a parent reading a card.
setup.caption: 2. Fill in each box with yes, no or maybe.

setup.art: The finished table with the boxes where the three tests disagree circled in red.
setup.caption: 3. Circle the rows where the tests disagree.

flow.do: Draw a table with three columns and eight rows. The columns are the seven signs, NASA's test and Koshland's pillars. The rows are a flame, a salt crystal, a dry seed and a mule. The last four are a virus, a curd bacterium, a robot and a forest fire. Before you fill in anything, ask your child to guess which two cases the tests will disagree about, and write the guess.
flow.say: We will use three real tests on eight cases. Test one is the seven signs, which you know. Test two is NASA's. Test three is Koshland's seven pillars.
flow.kid: Draw a table. Three tests go across the top. Eight cases go down the side.
flow.parent: The three tests in plain words. The seven signs: it feeds, breathes, grows, moves, senses, gets rid of waste and makes young. NASA's test: it is a chemical system that keeps itself going, and its kind can change by Darwin's rules over many generations. Koshland's pillars: it has instructions, it improvises when conditions change, it has a skin that makes compartments, it uses energy, it regenerates, it adapts and it keeps its chemical reactions apart.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Tests, Eight Cases. You draw the table.

flow.do: Go down the table one case at a time. For each of the three tests, ask 'does it pass?' and write yes, no or maybe. Use the notes below to help.
flow.say: For each case, ask: does this pass the seven signs? Does it pass NASA's test? Does it pass Koshland's pillars? Write yes, no or maybe.
flow.kid: For each case, ask if it passes each test. Write yes, no or maybe.
flow.parent: A guide to the boxes. Flame: no, no, no. Salt crystal: no, no, no. Dry seed: maybe, yes, maybe, because the seven signs are not all seen while resting, and the seed is resting. Mule: yes with one exception on young, yes as part of the horse and donkey lines, yes. Virus: no, maybe, no. Curd bacterium: yes, yes, yes. Robot: no, no, no. Forest fire: no, no, no. Accept good reasons for different answers. Two or more children: each child fills in one column for all eight cases, then you compare columns. With one child, the parent fills in the columns the child does not know yet.

check.q: A mule almost never has young, but passes NASA's test as part of the horse and donkey lines. Why?
options: The test is about a kind of living thing over many generations, not each single body
A mule is secretly not alive
NASA made an error
check.why: NASA's test asks if a system can evolve, which is a feature of a kind across generations. A single mule is a member of lines that do.

flow.context: In this step, you fill in the table with your child.

flow.do: Look for the rows where the three tests do not agree. Circle them. Ask which tests are fooled and why. Compare with the guess made at the start.
flow.say: Look at each row. Do the three tests agree? Circle the rows where they disagree. Why do you think they disagree?
flow.kid: Circle the rows where the tests disagree. Why do they disagree?
flow.parent: The rows that usually disagree are the dry seed and the virus. The seed passes NASA's test but is not doing all seven signs while resting. The virus evolves, but she needs a host cell. After the child has said their view, explain: scientists do not pick one test. They use all three as tools and look at where they disagree, because that is where they learn something.
flow.think: Which of the three tests do you trust most? Why?
flow.context: In this step, you find the cases that scientists argue about.

activities.title: Spot the Thermostats: machines that keep something steady

materials.item: a pencil and paper
the machines in your home, such as a fridge, a water heater or geyser, an electric iron and an air conditioner or rice cooker

schedule.what: Find four machines that keep something steady. For each, find what it senses, what it switches, and where its energy comes from.

activities.record: A table with four machines. For each machine write what it keeps steady, what it senses, what it switches on or off, and where its energy comes from. Add a row for your own body.
activities.context: In this activity, you find machines in your home that keep something steady. Then you compare them with your own body, which does the same.

setup.art: A child walking through a kitchen pointing at a fridge, a rice cooker and an electric iron, with a notebook in hand.
setup.caption: 1. Find four machines that keep something steady.

setup.art: A table with columns for keeps steady, senses, switches and energy from, with two rows filled in.
setup.caption: 2. For each machine, fill in what it keeps steady, senses and switches.

setup.art: A body outline beside a fridge, with matching arrows for sensing, switching and energy.
setup.caption: 3. Fill in a row for your own body.

flow.do: Walk through the house with your child. Find four machines that keep something steady. A fridge keeps cold. A geyser keeps water hot. An iron keeps its heat. A rice cooker clicks off when the rice is done.
flow.say: Many machines keep one thing steady. A fridge keeps cold. A geyser keeps water hot. Find four machines at home. Write down what each one keeps steady.
flow.kid: Find four machines that keep something steady. Write what each keeps steady.

ask.q: How does the machine know when to switch on or off?

flow.parent: Any machine that holds a temperature works. Do not open any machine or touch a hot iron. Keep to looking at the dials and the lights. Only a grown-up touches plugs, the geyser or the iron, and nobody opens a machine. Before the walk, ask your child to guess which machines will have a thermostat. If you have no geyser or AC, use a fridge, an iron, a rice cooker or pressure cooker, an electric kettle that clicks off, or a ceiling fan with a regulator for comparison.
flow.context: This is the first step of Spot the Thermostats. You find four machines.

flow.do: For each machine, ask three questions. What does it sense? What does it switch on or off? Where does the energy come from? Write the answers in the table.
flow.say: For each machine ask three things. What does it sense? What does it switch on or off? Where does its energy come from?
flow.kid: For each machine: What does it sense? What does it switch? Where does its energy come from?
flow.parent: A fridge senses the temperature inside, switches the cooling on and off, and gets its energy from electricity. A geyser senses the water temperature, switches the heater, and uses electricity. The inside of a machine like this is called a thermostat. Two to four children: each child takes one machine and reports to the others. With one child, do two machines yourself and let the child do the rest.

check.q: Which part of a fridge works like your skin sensing that you are cold?
options: The thermostat, which senses the temperature
The door
The light inside
check.why: A thermostat senses the temperature and tells the machine to switch on or off. Your skin and brain do the same job for your body.

flow.context: In this step, you take each machine apart in your head.

flow.do: Add a row for your own body. Ask what the body senses, what it switches and where its energy comes from. Then ask what a fridge can do that a living body can do, and what it cannot.
flow.say: Now fill in a row for you. What does your body sense? What does it switch on or off? Where does your energy come from?
flow.kid: Fill in a row for your body. What does it sense? What does it switch? Where is the energy from?
flow.parent: The body senses with skin and nerves, switches sweating, shivering and blood flow, and gets energy from food. After your child has answered, explain: a fridge was built by people and powered from outside. It cannot build its parts from other materials, and it cannot mend itself or make a new fridge. So keeping steady is one of the traits of life, but not enough on its own.
flow.think: A fridge keeps steady as well as you do. So why is a fridge not alive?
flow.context: In this step, you compare a machine with your own body.

projects.title: Cut It Up: which pieces start again?

materials.item: a money plant (pothos) stem about 15 centimetres long, cut by a grown-up just below a node, which is the knob where a leaf joins. No money plant? A mint (pudina) or coleus stem with a node works the same way
a single money plant leaf, cut off with a short stalk and no node
a potato that has started to sprout, from the back of the kitchen cupboard (a smooth potato piece with no eye is the second piece)
2 clear glasses and a plate
kitchen tissue and a lidded dabba. Leave the lid slightly open
a knife, used by a grown-up
a small magnifying glass, if you have one

projects.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Never eat a sprouting or green potato, because it can make you ill. Wash your hands after touching the potato. Throw rotted potato in the dustbin, and do not smell it closely.

schedule.what: Guess, then set up the money plant cuttings in water and the potato pieces on damp tissue in the dabba.
Look at everything. Top up the water and wet the tissue.
Look again. Measure roots and sprouts, and write what you see.
Look at everything one last time, compare, and say what the evidence shows.

projects.record: A table with one row for each piece: the stem with a node, the leaf alone, the potato piece with an eye, the potato piece without an eye. For each day write what you see, such as roots, sprouts or rot. Draw each piece on day 1 and day 10.
projects.context: In this project, you cut living things into pieces and find out which pieces can start again. A broken salt crystal grows in every piece, but a living thing needs more.

setup.art: A money plant stem standing in a glass of water, with a single leaf lying in water in a second glass.
setup.caption: 1. Put the stem with a node in one glass, and the single leaf in another.

setup.art: A sprouting potato cut into two pieces by a grown-up, one piece with a pale sprout and one without.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up cuts the potato into a piece with an eye and a piece without.

setup.art: Two potato pieces on damp tissue in a closed dabba in a dark cupboard.
setup.caption: 3. Put both potato pieces on damp tissue in the dabba, in a dark place.

setup.art: A child's notebook with four rows and drawings of the pieces on day 1 and day 10.
setup.caption: 4. Draw each piece, then look at them on day 3, day 6 and day 10.

flow.do: Show your child the stem, the single leaf and the potato. Ask which pieces they think will start again, and why. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: We will cut up a plant and a potato. Which pieces will start growing again? Which will not? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which pieces will start growing again? Which will not? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think the leaf alone will not grow roots?
good: It has no place to grow from.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. A stem with a node usually roots in water in one to three weeks. A leaf alone usually goes yellow without rooting. A potato piece with an eye sprouts in the damp dark in a week or two. A piece without an eye usually does little or goes soft.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cut It Up. You guess before you start.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the potato into a piece with an eye and a piece without. Put the stem and the leaf in separate glasses of water. Let the cut potato pieces dry in the air for an hour. Lay them on damp tissue in the dabba, and put the lid on loosely.
flow.say: A grown-up does the cutting. The stem and the leaf go in water. The potato pieces go on damp tissue in the dabba, in a dark place.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the potato. Put the stem and the leaf in water. Put the potato pieces in the dabba.
flow.parent: Put the glasses on a bright windowsill, but not in direct hot sun. In hot, wet weather a closed damp dabba rots potato quickly, so keep the lid loose. Change the water in the glasses every three days. Two to four children: one set each, or one child per piece; each draws and measures their own, with the grown-up doing the cutting. Keep the potato dabba in a cupboard. Check the tissue is damp but not soaking. Label each piece with a small piece of paper.

check.q: Why do we keep all four pieces in similar places, with water or damp tissue?
options: So any difference comes from the piece itself
So they look neat
So they do not smell
check.why: A fair test changes one thing at a time. If one piece were dry, we would not know whether the piece or the dryness made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you set up all four pieces.

flow.do: Look at everything and write what you see. Top up the water and wet the tissue if it has dried.
flow.say: Look at each piece. Is anything new growing? Write down what you see. Top up the water.
flow.kid: Look at each piece. Is anything growing? Write what you see.
flow.parent: Not much will have happened by day 3. That is normal. Write 'nothing yet' if so.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the pieces on day 3.

flow.do: Look again. Measure any roots or sprouts with a ruler and write the lengths. Notice which pieces have changed and which have not.
flow.say: Look closely. Use a magnifying glass for tiny roots. Which pieces are changing? Which are not?
flow.kid: Look closely. Measure any roots or sprouts. Which pieces are changing?
flow.parent: A money plant stem may show small white roots or bumps by now, or only in a week more. Roots can take two to three weeks, so on day 10 small white bumps are a good result. If nothing has changed in a piece, keep it going for a few more days. If a potato piece has gone soft and smelly, throw it away and write 'rotted'. That is a result too.
flow.context: In this step, you measure the pieces on day 6.

flow.do: Look at everything one last time. Draw each piece again. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Draw each piece again. Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw each piece again. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the stem with a node and the potato piece with an eye started again, and that the leaf alone and the potato without an eye did not. After they have said what they saw, explain: a piece can start again if it has a growing point, such as a node or an eye, and enough stored food to live on until new roots or leaves can feed it. This is called regeneration. A crystal piece has no growing point, because it just keeps stacking.
flow.think: A broken salt crystal grows in every piece. Why do only some pieces of a living thing start again?
flow.context: In this step, you compare all four pieces on day 10 and say what the evidence shows.

challenges.title: The Faker: design a non-living thing that fools the most tests
challenges.problem: Design a pretend creature, or a machine, that is not alive but passes as many tests for life as possible. Then design the opposite: a living thing that fails as many tests as possible but is still alive.
constraints: Your faker must not be alive. It can be made of fire, crystals, metal, plastic, a computer or anything non-living.
Use the seven signs of life as your tests: feeds, breathes, grows, moves, senses, gets rid of waste, makes young.
Draw or build your faker with a label for each test it passes.
Your sleeper must be a real living thing that really exists.
materials: scrap cardboard, foil, tape and scissors, if you want to build a model
the list of the seven signs of life
general: A candle flame: it uses fuel and air, grows, moves and spreads.
A robot with sensors and wheels that moves, senses and charges itself.
A crystal garden: it grows and copies its pattern.
A forest fire that eats, grows and travels.
creative: A robot that builds a copy of itself from spare parts, an idea the mathematician John von Neumann worked on in the 1940s.
A pattern in a computer, such as a glider in John Conway's Game of Life, that moves across a grid and makes copies.
A fire that is fed by a machine, kept at a steady heat by a thermostat and made to spread by a fan, so it passes almost every sign of life.
For the sleeper, a seed or a tardigrade that dries up, passes almost none of the signs, and wakes again.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your faker and your sleeper. Count how many of the seven signs each one passes. Then say which sign was the hardest to fake, and which test you would add to catch your faker.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about tests for life. You build a non-living thing that fools the tests, and a living thing that fails them.
